TCE 504 • Applied Exercise Physiology
05 / ENERGY & ATP
PART 1 • WHAT IS ATP?

ATP is the immediate energy currency.

Start with the molecule itself. Focus on its structure and its role in cellular work.

THINK BEFORE MOVING ON
What is the key reason ATP is so important during exercise?
PART 2 • ATP HYDROLYSIS

ATP powers muscle contraction.

Now zoom into the working muscle: ATP hydrolysis releases energy that supports the cross-bridge cycle and contraction.

STOP & THINK
If ATP is continually used during exercise, what must happen next?
PART 3 • THREE ENERGY SYSTEMS

Three systems — one common goal: resynthesise ATP.

Read each system separately. They work at the same time, but their relative contribution changes with exercise demand.

PART 4 • SUBSTRATES FOR EACH SYSTEM

What does each system use?

Before comparing pathways, identify the major substrates and whether oxygen is required.

PART 5 • WHERE DO THE SUBSTRATES GO?

Cytosol or mitochondrion?

Follow the substrate into the cell. The location of metabolism helps explain why different pathways have different characteristics.

CHECK
Which location is central to oxidative metabolism?
PART 6 • KEY COMPARISON

Compare the three systems.

Use the table to connect substrate, rate, capacity, oxygen requirement and typical exercise context.

Rate

How quickly ATP can be regenerated.

Capacity

How much total ATP the pathway can support.

Contribution

Relative contribution changes with intensity, duration and exercise nature.

PART 7 • APPLY IT — 400-M RUNNER

Now apply the energy-system story.

Watch how ATP demand and pathway contribution change as the 400-m run progresses.

Key take-home message

The energy systems do not switch on and off like separate buttons. ATP-PCr, glycolytic and oxidative pathways all contribute, while their relative contribution changes as exercise demand changes.

STARTATP demand rises immediately and rapid ATP resynthesis is required.
EARLY EFFORTATP-PCr contribution is important, with glycolytic contribution increasing.
CONTINUINGGlycolytic and oxidative contributions become increasingly important alongside the phosphagen system.
